opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's actually one of the main things we worked on after the original HippoRAG paper. We found that the graph approach was great at multi-hop, associative questions, the kind where you have to connect two pieces of information that never appear in the same document. But on simpler factual questions, standard dense retrieval was sometimes better. The graph alone was losing some of the contextual richness that an embedding of the full passage captures.

So the way we brought them together was to put the passages into the graph itself. In the original version, the knowledge graph was just the phrase nodes, the entities and concepts we extracted with an LLM using open information extraction, plus the edges between them. In the newer version we also add the passages as nodes and connect each one to the phrases that came from it. Now you have a single structure that holds both the fine-grained conceptual links and the dense, contextual chunks of text.

At query time, we still run personalized PageRank, but we change how we seed it. Before, we picked out entities from the query and started the random walk from the matching phrase nodes. Now we also run standard dense retrieval over the passages, and those similarity scores become part of the reset probabilities. So the walk starts from both the concepts the query points to and the passages that semantically match it, and it spreads from there. Dense retrieval sets up a good starting point, and the graph propagation lets you reach passages that are connected but wouldn't have scored highly on similarity by themselves.

We made a couple of other changes too. Instead of matching just entities from the query, we match the whole query against triples, which captures more of what the question is actually asking. And we added a filtering step, which we think of as something like recognition memory. An LLM looks at the candidate triples and removes the irrelevant ones before they seed the graph search, so you don't spread activation from noise.

What we were happy to see is that the combined system didn't give up performance on the simple factual benchmarks, which had been the weak point, and it improved on the associative and sense-making tasks. That fits the bigger goal. We want something closer to how human long-term memory works, where you have the raw episodes and also the web of associations that links them, and retrieval draws on both.

r001.rationale: The response says dense retrieval similarity scores become part of PageRank reset probabilities, but does not say the retrieval scores are normalized and combined.

r002.rationale: It describes adding passage nodes linked to phrases and spreading activation through the graph, but does not explain that this can spread PageRank probability mass too broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we actually think about a lot, because I don't see the two as being in competition. Standard RAG with dense embeddings is really good at one thing, which is finding passages that are semantically similar to your query. If you ask a question and there's a paragraph somewhere that basically answers it directly, embedding retrieval will find it. Where it struggles is when the answer is spread across multiple documents, and the connection between them isn't obvious from the query alone. That's the multi-hop case, and that's really what HippoRAG was designed for.

So the way we think about combining them is pretty natural, and it actually mirrors what the hippocampus-neocortex story suggests. In HippoRAG, the knowledge graph is kind of this sparse, associative index. You extract entities and relations from your passages, you link entities to the passages they came from, and then at query time you identify the entities in the question, seed Personalized PageRank from those nodes, and let the activation spread through the graph. The passages that light up are the ones that are connected to your query entities, even if they don't look semantically similar to the question.

But the graph has a weakness, which is that it's built on named entities. If your question is more about a concept or a description, or if entity extraction missed something, the graph won't have good seed nodes to start from. And that's exactly where dense retrieval is strong.

So the simplest combination, and honestly the one I'd recommend people start with, is to run both and fuse the results. You get a ranked list from your embedding retriever, you get a ranked list from the PageRank scores over passages, and you combine them, either with something like reciprocal rank fusion or by learning a weighting. In practice, we found that this hybrid tends to be strictly better than either one alone, because the failure modes are pretty complementary. Dense retrieval covers the single-hop, paraphrase-heavy cases, and the graph covers the cases where you need to traverse.

The more interesting version, and this is where we went with the follow-up work, is to actually integrate them more tightly rather than just fusing at the end. One thing you can do is use dense retrieval to find your seed nodes instead of relying purely on exact entity matching. So you embed the entity nodes in the graph, you embed the query, and you pick seed nodes by similarity. That makes the graph retrieval much more robust to how the question is phrased. Another thing is to add the passages themselves as nodes in the graph, connected to the entities they mention, and then dense retrieval similarity can act as another type of edge or as an initial score on those passage nodes before you run PageRank. So you're essentially letting the semantic signal and the structural signal interact during the random walk rather than only at the end.

I think the mental model I'd leave people with is: dense retrieval tells you where to start, and the graph tells you where to go from there. Embeddings give you good entry points into the corpus, and the associative structure lets you reach the things that are related but not lexically or semantically obvious. When you set it up that way, you're not really picking between RAG and HippoRAG, you're using each one for the part of the problem it's actually good at.

r001.rationale: The response proposes fusing ranked results with reciprocal rank fusion or learned weighting, but does not specify combining normalized retrieval scores.

r002.rationale: It proposes adding passage nodes connected to entities, but does not say this can spread personalized PageRank probability mass too broadly.

astra-6.text:
I’d treat them as complementary retrieval signals. Standard RAG is good at finding passages that are semantically similar to the question. HippoRAG adds the ability to follow connections between entities, which can surface relevant passages that don’t look similar to the question directly.

You could run both in parallel, combine their candidate passages, and then rerank them before giving them to the language model. That gives you the direct matches from semantic retrieval and the more indirect connections from graph retrieval.

A tighter integration would use semantic retrieval to help initialize the graph search. Instead of starting only from entities identified in the question, you could also use the retrieved passages as evidence about where to start. Then graph retrieval expands from those starting points. The important thing is to preserve the strong direct retrieval signal while allowing the graph to bring in information you would otherwise miss.

r001.rationale: It proposes combining candidate passages and reranking them, but does not say to combine normalized retrieval scores.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss adding document nodes connected to constituent entities or personalized PageRank probability mass spreading across the graph.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Standard RAG is good at finding passages that are semantically similar to your question. HippoRAG adds a way to connect information across passages, even when those passages aren’t individually that similar to the question.

One way to combine them is to use semantic retrieval to provide starting points for the graph search. You retrieve relevant passages, use those to help identify promising nodes in the graph, and then let the graph retrieval expand toward related information. You can also run the two in parallel and combine their rankings before passing the retrieved passages to the language model.

The intuition is that you want both signals: direct semantic relevance and relevance that comes from connections. For a straightforward question, the semantic retriever might already give you everything you need. For a question that requires bringing together multiple facts, the graph can help surface the missing pieces.

r001.rationale: The response suggests combining rankings from the two retrieval methods, but does not say to combine normalized retrieval scores.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss document nodes connected to constituent entities or their effect on personalized PageRank probability mass.
